floorplan3d · team walkthrough

From a 2D floor-plan image to a 3D model

How one AutoCAD-style house plan went through the offline floorplan3d pipeline, step by step. Every picture on this page was produced from that plan by the pipeline's own code.

Input
2248 × 2373 px PNG
Scale
31 px/ft (101.7 px/m)
Detected
11 rooms · 49 walls
Openings
14 doors · 12 windows
Runtime
≈ 49 s on laptop CPU

The pipeline at a glance

The tool runs fully offline on the CPU. There is one neural network (a small U-Net) and one OCR engine. Everything else is classic image processing and geometry. The entry point is analyze() in floorplan3d/pipeline.py.

00

Set up the environment

The project is plain Python. All packages install once from requirements.txt into a local virtual environment in .venv. After that, no internet connection is needed.

The README asks for Python 3.9–3.12. Our machine only had 3.13, and installing another version through winget was blocked by Group Policy. We tried 3.13 and every package installed and ran correctly, so we kept it.

# one time, in the project folder
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\python -m pip install -r requirements.txt

# check the install on the bundled sample
run_windows.bat sample_plan.png

numpy, opencv, onnxruntimerapidocr_onnxruntimeshapely, trimesh

01

Upload and prepare the plan

The input is an ordinary image file. This one is a clean, AutoCAD-style drawing: thick black walls, arc doors, triple-line windows, and room names with sizes printed inside the rooms.

Before running it, we cropped 20 px from every edge. The original image has a thin grey frame around it. In the first run, the pipeline read that frame as an outer wall, so the whole page background became one huge "room".

Lesson: look at the input before you run anything. Borders, title blocks, logos and stamps all look like walls to the model.

cv2.imdecode → BGR arraypipeline.py · analyze()
02

Read the text (OCR)

RapidOCR, the PaddleOCR models running on ONNX Runtime, finds every text box and reads it. Each string is then sorted into one of three groups:

  • Room names are matched against keywords for 15 room types, such as "Bed Room" → bedroom and "Pantry" → kitchen.
  • Dimension strings, such as 18' 3", are used later to work out the scale.
  • Other text is kept in the JSON but not used.

On this plan, OCR found 15 strings, including all 13 room names and "Up" for the stairs. It found no usable dimension strings. That turns out to matter a lot in the next step.

floorplan3d/ocr.pyread_text(), room_type_from_text()
03

Find the scale (pixels per metre)

Every measurement depends on knowing how many pixels make up one metre. The pipeline tries three methods, in this order:

  • Dimension lines. Match each dimension string to its drawn line and measure the line between its arrowheads. This is the most accurate method, typically within 1%.
  • Door widths. If there are no dimension lines, assume a typical door is 0.85 m wide.
  • Wall thickness. If no doors are found either, assume walls are 0.15 m thick.

This plan has no dimension lines, so the first run fell back to door widths. It guessed 4.84 px/ft, which is about 6× too small, and every size came out wrong.

The fix was to supply the scale ourselves. The 15'-wide bedroom measures about 466 px between its inner wall faces, and 466 ÷ 15 ≈ 31 px/ft.

.venv\Scripts\python -m floorplan3d autocad_plan.png ^
    -o output --scale-px-per-ft 31
floorplan3d/dimensions.py · calibrate()--scale-px-per-ft / --scale-px-per-m
04

Segment every pixel (U-Net)

A small U-Net (2.2 M parameters, 9 MB ONNX file) gives every pixel one of 11 classes. The model was trained at about 55 px/m. Because we know our scale (101.7 px/m), the image is first shrunk by 0.54× so the walls look as thick as they did in training.

The model runs three times, on the original, a left-right flip and an up-down flip, and the results are averaged. This is called test-time augmentation and makes the masks steadier. --fast turns it off.

Notice that the walls, doors and windows are clean, but the room colours are patchy. That is expected. Room types come mainly from the OCR labels, and the model's room guess is only a fallback.

walldoorwindow livingkitchenbedroom bathroombalcony
floorplan3d/segment.py · segment()models/floorplan_seg.onnx
05

Clean the masks

The probabilities are split into separate wall, door and window masks. These are refined using the actual black ink of the drawing, and small specks are removed. Wall thickness is then measured from the wall mask using the typical run length of wall pixels. Here it is 28 px ≈ 0.28 m.

Furniture, stairs and the kitchen island are mostly gone at this point, because the model was trained to ignore them.

walldoorwindow
vectorize.py · clean_masks(), wall_thickness_px()
06

Turn wall pixels into wall lines

3D software needs lines, not pixels. Each wall becomes a straight horizontal or vertical centre-line with a thickness. The steps are:

  • Fit horizontal and vertical runs of wall pixels.
  • Snap wall ends together where they meet, and split walls at T-junctions.
  • Close tiny breaks (under 0.45 m). A gap the size of a door becomes a door opening instead.
  • Drop short stubs and blobs that don't belong to a wall.

Result: 49 wall segments. Diagonal or curved walls are not supported yet; they would be broken into straight steps.

extract_walls(), find_wall_gaps()drop_stubs(), join_small_gaps()
07

Attach doors and windows to walls

Each door or window mask is assigned to the wall it sits on. The pipeline records where it starts along that wall and how wide it is. Openings narrower than 0.3 m for doors, or 0.25 m for windows, are dropped as noise.

This is what lets the 3D export cut real holes in the walls. A door has a sill at 0 m and a head at 2.1 m. A window has its sill at 0.9 m and its head at 2.1 m.

Result: 14 doors and 12 windows. Two of the "doors" are false: the open front and side of the porch were read as wide doorways (7' 8" and 5' 1").

vectorize.py · extract_openings()
08

Find the rooms

A room is an area of floor enclosed by walls. Open doorways would let rooms leak into each other, so short "virtual walls" are drawn across them first. The remaining enclosed regions are labelled with connected-component analysis. Anything connected to the image edge is outside the building.

This found 10 regions inside the building. Dining, Living and Foyer form one region because no walls separate them on the drawing. The Covered Patio sits outside the walls (shown white), so it is added later as a balcony from its OCR label. That brings the final count to 11.

virtual_walls(), extract_rooms()pipeline.py · _merge_unsupported_splits()
09

Name the rooms and convert to metres

Each OCR room name is dropped into the region that contains it, and the name sets the room type. The segmentation model's vote is used only when a room has no label. Every pixel coordinate is then divided by the scale to give metres. Polygons, areas and perimeters are measured from each region's outline.

Walls are marked exterior when one side faces the outside, and interior otherwise.

10

Export the JSON and 3D files

Everything is written to one JSON file in metres, schema floorplan3d/v1. Any 3D tool can rebuild the house from it. The pipeline's own exporter, export3d.py, does this with trimesh:

  • Extrude each wall as a box: length × 2.75 m height × thickness.
  • Split the box around each opening, leaving the part above a door and the parts above and below a window.
  • Triangulate each room polygon into a floor, coloured by room type.
  • Save as .glb and .obj, render a preview PNG, and write an offline three.js viewer page.
{ "id": "D1", "type": "door", "wall_id": "W37",
  "offset_from_wall_start_m": 0.315, "width_m": 0.806,
  "height_m": 2.1, "sill_height_m": 0.0,
  "connects": ["R1", "R2"] }

Known issues on this plan

Open-plan merge

Dining, Living and Foyer come out as one 1180 ft² "Living" room. The drawing has no walls between them, and the region splitter needs wall corners to cut along.

Porch "doors"

The porch's open front and side were read as 7' 8" and 5' 1" doorways. Open sides of outdoor areas look like wall gaps to the gap detector.

3D floor triangles

The large L-shaped living floor shows stray triangles in the 3D preview. shapely.ops.triangulate triangulates the polygon's points, not its outline, so concave shapes can get triangles outside the room.

Kitchen counter

The kitchen counter and island aren't labelled, so the kitchen merges into the living area. Only the Pantry is typed as kitchen.

Checklist for your own plans

Before running

  • Crop off borders, title blocks, logos and stamps.
  • Use a clean drawing, at least about 800 px wide. Straighten phone photos first.
  • Check whether the plan has dimension lines or only room-size labels.

After running

  • Read the scale line in the console. If it says estimated … (verify!), don't trust the sizes.
  • Compare two or three detected rooms with the sizes printed on the plan.
  • Open _detected.png and look for walls that aren't really walls.

Handy flags

--scale-px-per-ft 31   # known scale
--wall-height 3.0      # metres
--fast                 # ~3x faster
--no-3d                # PNG + JSON only
--no-ocr               # skip text
